items.title: Storm Harry: Drifting buoys help improve early forecasts of extreme events in the Mediterranean Sea
items.summary: A network of drifting buoys equipped with barometers can help improve weather forecasts of extreme Mediterranean storms by providing crucial atmospheric observations from areas of the sea where measurements are scarce. A new study published in the Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society provides the first assessment of the impact of these observations during Storm Harry, which affected the Mediterranean region in January 2026.

items.title: Local DNA motion inside the cell stays nearly constant throughout interphase
items.summary: Human genomic DNA is wrapped around core histone proteins to form nucleosomes, the fundamental units of chromatin. During interphase, the period between cell divisions, DNA is replicated and the nucleus becomes larger. At the same time, cells must continuously carry out essential genome functions such as transcription, DNA replication and DNA repair. How the behavior of genomic DNA is maintained during these large changes has remained unclear.

items.title: Additional ionization during nuclear $\beta^{\pm}$ decay in atomic systems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An original method is developed for numerical calculations of probabilities of the bound-free atomic excitations during the nuclear $\beta^{\pm}$ decays in actual atoms and ions. To achieve this goal we have derived and tested the closed analytical formulas for the final state probabilities of different excitations in the few-electron atomic systems. This study is the first non-approximate and essentially complete investigation of the atomic bound-free excitations during the nuclear $\beta^{\pm}$ decays in atoms.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.14102v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is severely under-constrained by limited X-ray projections. Learned reconstruction can provide complementary anatomical information, but using it as a prior in patient-specific Gaussian reconstruction introduces two challenges. items.summary: arXiv:2610.14105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate artery extraction from X-ray coronary angiography (XCA) is essential for coronary artery disease diagnosis and intervention. However, low vessel visibility, respiratory and cardiac motion, and limited annotations challenge existing methods. Moreover, most deep learning approaches produce binary vessel masks without preserving clinically relevant intra-arterial contrast information. items.summary: arXiv:2610.14138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retinal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of ophthalmic tasks, yet relatively little is known about how disease-related information is represented within their learned embeddings and whether this distribution influences downstream prediction performance. items.summary: arXiv:2610.16595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surface-based cortical analysis is useful in many applications as it is a natural way to model the highly folded structure of the cerebral cortex, allowing quantities such as curvature and thickness to be easily calculated. items.summary: arXiv:2610.17950v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traditional optical system design for imaging applications has long been guided by image quality metrics such as geometrical RMS spot size, wavefront error, and modulation transfer function (MTF). items.summary: arXiv:2610.13956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn world models by predicting future representations rather than reconstructing observations. items.summary: arXiv:2610.13966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting cellular responses to chemical and genetic perturbations is a central test for AI virtual cells, yet many single-cell models reduce each condition to an average expression shift. items.summary: arXiv:2610.13982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as an effective paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their massive parameter footprint poses severe memory challenges for deployment. items.summary: arXiv:2610.13990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse attention visits few keys, yet finding them can still require scoring every key with every indexer head. items.summary: arXiv:2610.13991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving agents improve through repeated cycles of modification and evaluation. However, existing methods receive feedback on modifications only after costly evaluations, and aggregate scores may obscure distinctions between failures that require different repairs. items.summary: arXiv:2610.13995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. items.title: Enhanced Trading Systems with Intelligent Market Analysis
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid reinforcement learning trading framework integrating intraday market data with transformer-based financial sentiment signals. The system extracts sentiment dynamics and semantic event clusters from financial news and incorporates them into a PPO-based trading agent. Experiments on intraday NSE data demonstrate improved risk-adjusted returns compared to price-only baselines.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.14004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People often learn from others' demonstrations, and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) techniques have realized this capacity in machines. In contrast, teaching by demonstration has been less well studied computationally. Here, we develop a Bayesian model for teaching by demonstration. items.summary: arXiv:2610.14006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Since compact, interpretable classifiers correspond to simple programs, it is natural to ask if LLM-based coding agents can be used to learn interpretable models from data. items.summary: arXiv:2610.14009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large AI models increasingly rely on distributed GPU execution, yet it remains unclear whether established failure analysis methods transfer effectively to this setting. items.summary: arXiv:2610.14136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. items.summary: arXiv:2610.14146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon terminal benchmarks measure whether an agent can sustain progress through extended workflows with process rewards, not only whether its final state passes a binary check. items.summary: arXiv:2610.14149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: VETNET represents an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks designed to accelerate AI-driven innovation in animal science and veterinary medicine through standardized, high-quality datasets and multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. items.summary: arXiv:2610.14186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Could model-free reinforcement learning algorithms actually be learning a model of the environment? items.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Show HN: Guitoro, a virtual guitar you strum with your keyboard
items.summary: Guitoro is a free browser guitar using recordings of real instruments. You can strum with your keyboard, mouse, or touchscreen, choose acoustic, classical, electric guitar or bass, and see chord fingering and each stroke. Song practice can be slowed to 20%, and there are free chord tools and tuners. No signup or download. 1 minute video demo: https://youtu.be/DtcluMLdSgs I would love feedback on how the strumming feels and sounds. items.title: [Editorial] Rethinking lived experience
items.summary: The theme of this year's World Mental Health Day, held on Oct 10, is Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change. On its website, WHO states that the voices of people with lived experience should “shape the policies, services and decisions that affect their lives”. While these are laudable aims, they also serve to highlight the complex challenges involved in lived experience engagement and co-production, both within the field of mental health and beyond.

items.title: [Comment] Retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes: what have we learned from TRIUMPH-2?
items.summary: It is a general observation that the degree of weight loss obtained with GLP-1 receptor agonists is less in individuals with type 2 diabetes than in people without diabetes and similar BMI. Could this difference be overcome with the new triple agonists with superior weight-lowering effects? The TRIUMPH-2 study by Virginia Bellido and colleagues1 in The Lancet is a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial of the effects of retatrutide, a triple agonist (GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon), in people with obesity and type 2 diabetes.

items.title: [Comment] Closing the gap on mortality for adolescents living with HIV

items.title: [Comment] Offline: Medicine for peace
items.summary: Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) is most famous for his line in Leviathan (1651) that, “the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”. That proposition may have been true in 17th-century England, but, thanks to the evolution and expansion of health systems, it is not so today for many, although obviously not all. But abstracting that line alone is to miss Hobbes’ wider views about the nature of human being. He believed that without a “common power” ruling over society, our natural tendency is “that condition which is called war…of every man against every man”.

items.title: [Correspondence] Regulate prospective development of medical AI now
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing through medicine at a pace that regulation, ethics, and professional reflection have struggled to match. The prevailing assumption appears to be that if a technology can be developed, it should be developed—and that its place in clinical care can be debated afterwards. We believe this sequence should be reversed.

items.title: [Correspondence] The health literacy crisis in the age of AI: lessons from PISA 2025
items.summary: The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) results should concern the health community.1 PISA does not measure health literacy directly, but it assesses several cognitive competencies that increasingly underpin people's ability to navigate health information. For example, in 2025, more than 760 000 students aged 15 years, from 91 countries and economies, participated in the assessment.1 The findings reveal a worrying deterioration in reading, mathematics, and science performance.

items.title: [Correspondence] Taiwan's path to hepatitis C elimination
items.summary: WHO has established a global target to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030.1 Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remains one of the leading causes of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality, affecting an estimated 50 million people worldwide.2 By integrating a comprehensive screening-to-cure cascade, HCV elimination has become an achievable public health goal.

items.title: [Correspondence] Personalising maintenance after tirzepatide weight loss
items.summary: Deborah B Horn and colleagues’ SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN trial provides important evidence that continued tirzepatide is superior to treatment withdrawal for maintaining pharmacologically induced weight loss.1 The trial also shows that reducing tirzepatide to 5 mg offers substantially greater protection against weight regain than switching to placebo. However, the trial's mean effects might not fully convey an important clinical message: response to lower-dose maintenance was heterogeneous.

items.title: [Correspondence] How much can ASTRUM-006 tell us?
items.summary: Lin Shen and colleagues report improved event-free survival with perioperative serplulimab in PD-L1-positive resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma.1 The trial is valuable: it selects patients by combined positive score and tests a chemotherapy-free adjuvant phase. However, we urge caution before it is read as practice-changing.

items.summary: We thank Osman Bilge Kaya and Berkan Karabuğa for their insightful comments regarding ASTRUM-006.1 We agree that some aspects need further clarification.

items.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial
items.summary: Michal F Kaminski and colleagues report that colonoscopy screening reduced colorectal cancer incidence, but not mortality, during a 13-year follow-up.1 The response from the public health field will focus, as it always does, on mortality. We think this focus misses the point of the trial.

items.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial
items.summary: In their recent Article, Michal F Kaminski and colleagues reported the effects of offering one-time screening colonoscopy at ages 55–64 years after a 13-year follow-up of the NordICC trial.1 Their findings should be interpreted in the context that this trial of a one-time offer of screening colonoscopy was conducted in an era of widespread use of colonoscopy in clinical practice. Estimated reductions in the incidence and mortality of colorectal cancer were much lower than anticipated at trial design.

items.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial
items.summary: The NordICC trial1 should be considered in context with previous colorectal cancer screening studies.2,3 Four randomised controlled trials with more than 458 000 participants show consistent colorectal cancer incidence reductions of 18–23% and larger colorectal cancer mortality reductions of 22–31% with sigmoidoscopy (appendix).3 In the NordICC trial, screening reduced colorectal cancer incidence but not mortality.1

items.title: Wood Street Steps in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
items.summary: The Wood Street Steps are the last surviving examples of 10 or more stairways Philadelphia founder William Penn commissioned along the original Delaware Riverbank. Why are they important? Penn felt all citizens should have public access to the river wharves. Some early wealthy Quakers, who owned land there, disagreed. As part of a 1684 compromise, Penn made sure at least 10 stairways led to the port area near major cross streets ... from Vine Street to what was originally called Cedar Street ... and is now known as South Street. Unfortunately, this is the only set of those steps left.
